rendering.persona_description: Keisha is a 24-year-old transgender woman working as a junior graphic designer at a small print shop. She's meticulous about her work, which her boss appreciates, though she knows privately it takes her far longer than it should. She lives with a roommate she's known since college and likes her, even though the living arrangement has become a source of tension lately.
rendering.clinical_context: Keisha has obsessive-compulsive disorder centered on symmetry and exactness: she needs objects aligned, actions repeated evenly on both sides, and things to feel 'balanced' or she gets a sense that something bad or unfinished will happen. Symptoms started around age 15 with straightening her school supplies and have grown over the years to include arranging her apartment, evening out physical sensations (touching one arm if she touched the other), and redoing tasks until they feel right. She did a course of exposure and response prevention a couple of years ago that helped for a while, but it ended over a year ago and she hasn't been in treatment since.
rendering.behavioral_description: She talks in careful, precise sentences, sometimes correcting herself mid-thought if a word choice feels 'off.' She's willing to consider what an assistant suggests, but she'll argue back if she thinks the suggestion doesn't respect how real the danger feels to her, since she genuinely believes that if things aren't even, something bad follows. She describes her compulsions matter-of-factly, without much self-flagellation, more like she's giving a status update.

traits.living_situation: shares an apartment with a longtime friend
traits.help_seeking_orientation: not currently seeking treatment, skeptical of reassurance she hasn't earned through her own effort
traits.cognitive_style: detail-focused, ruminative, treats felt asymmetry as evidence of real risk

clinical_history.presentation: obsessive-compulsive disorder, symmetry and exactness theme
clinical_history.history: Symptoms began around age 15 with straightening school supplies and evening out physical sensations, and gradually expanded to arranging her living space and redoing tasks at work. She did a course of exposure and response prevention that ended more than a year ago, after the checking and redoing had begun costing her significant time each day, but she has not been in treatment since.

symptoms: needing objects and furniture arranged symmetrically
evening out touch or sensation on both sides of her body
redoing tasks at work until they feel exactly right
intrusive sense that asymmetry will cause something bad to happen
occasionally resisting the urge to fix things on her own, with residual anxiety
